[[File:Acacia longifolia 03.jpg|thumb|Foliage and inflorescences]]

'''''Acacia longifolia''''' is a species of ''[[Acacia]]'' native to southeastern Australia, from the extreme southeast of [[Queensland]], eastern [[New South Wales]], eastern and southern [[Victoria, Australia|Victoria]], southeastern [[South Australia]], and [[Tasmania]]. Common names for it include '''long-leaved wattle''', '''acacia trinervis''', '''aroma doble''', '''golden wattle''', '''coast wattle''', '''sallow wattle''' and '''Sydney golden wattle'''. 

It is not listed as being a [[threatened species]],<ref name=anbg>Australian Plant Name Index: [http://www.anbg.gov.au/cgi-bin/apni?taxon_name=Acacia%20longifolia%25 ''Acacia longifolia''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230610072823/https://www.anbg.gov.au/cgi-bin/apni?taxon_name=Acacia%20longifolia%25 |date=2023-06-10 }}</ref><ref name=ILDIS/> and is considered [[Invasive species|invasive]] in Portugal, New Zealand<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-09-05 |title=Could a wasp join the fight in the war on weeds? |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/programmes/the-detail/story/2018857476/war-on-weeds-could-a-wasp-join-the-fight |access-date=2022-09-07 |website=[[RNZ]] |language=en-nz}}</ref> and South Africa.<ref name=jn>[https://web.archive.org/web/20080305011155/http://jn.sapo.pt/2007/10/07/sociedade_e_vida/vespa_australiana_pode_ajudar_a_redu.html Vespa australiana pode ajudar a reduzir invasão das acácias]</ref> In the southern region of [[Western Australia]], it has become naturalised and has been classed as a weed due to its out-competing indigenous species. It can grow very quickly, reaching 7–10 m in five to six years.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.warringah.nsw.gov.au/environment/tree_replace_small.aspx#acacialongifolia |title=Warringah Online |access-date=2007-04-21 |archive-date=2011-02-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110219010408/http://www.warringah.nsw.gov.au/environment/tree_replace_small.aspx#acacialongifolia }}</ref>

==Description==
Golden wattle occurs as a shrub or tree that can reach a height of up to {{cvt|8|m}}. It has smooth to finely fissured greyish coloured bark and [[glabrousness (botany)|glabrous]] branchlets that are angled towards the apices. Like most species of ''Acacia'' it has [[phyllode]]s rather than true leaves. The evergreen and glabrous phyllodes are mostly straight but occasionally slightly curved with a length of {{cvt|4|to|20|cm}} and a width of {{cvt|4|to|30|mm}} and have numerous prominent longitudinal veins.

It blooms between June and October in its native range, producing simple [[inflorescence]]s that occur singly or in pairs in the phyllode [[axil]]s on stalks with a length of less than {{cvt|2|mm}}. The cylindrical flower-spikes have a length of {{cvt|2|to|4.5|cm}} packed with bright to pale yellow coloured flowers.<ref name=NSW>{{cite web|url=https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl%26lvl=sp%26name=Acacia~longifolia|title=''Acacia longifolia'' (Andrews) Willd.|access-date=28 March 2020|work=PlantNet|publisher=[[Royal Botanic Garden, Sydney]]}}</ref> Following flowering thinly leathery to firmly papery [[seed pod]]s form that are straight to strongly twisted and raised over and constricted between each of the seeds. The pods are usually {{cvt|4|to|15|cm}} in length and {{cvt|2.5|to|6|mm}} and reasonably brittle when dry.<ref name=NSW/>

== Taxonomy ==
The species was first formally described in 1802 as ''Mimosa longifolia'' by [[Henry Cranke Andrews]], in ''The Botanist's Repository for New, and Rare Plants'', then as ''Acacia longifolia'' in 1806, in the [[Carl Ludwig Willdenow]] publication ''[[Species Plantarum]]''. It was reclassified as ''Racosperma longifolium'' in 1987 by [[Leslie Pedley]], but transferred back to genus ''Acacia'' in 2006. Other synonyms include ''Mimosa macrostachya'' and ''Phyllodoce longifolia''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://bie.ala.org.au/species/https://id.biodiversity.org.au/taxon/apni/51286955#names|title=''Acacia longifolia'' (Andrews) Willd.|access-date=29 March 2020|work=Atlas of Living Australia|publisher=[[Global Biodiversity Information Facility]]}}</ref>

The [[botanical name|specific epithet]] refers to the long phyllodes on the species.<ref name=NSW/>

There are two recognised [[subspecies]]:<ref name=anbg/>
*''Acacia longifolia'' subsp. ''longifolia''
*[[Acacia sophorae|''Acacia longifolia'' subsp. ''sophorae'' (Labill.) Court]]

==Distribution==
The species is [[endemism|endemic]] to coastal area of south eastern [[Queensland]] close to the border with New South Wales extending southward down the coast of [[New South Wales]]. In New South Wales it is common along the tablelands and coastal areas where it is situated in various habitats including foredunes and is usually a part of [[sclerophyll]]  woodland or coastal heath and scrub communities.<ref name=NSW/> The range then extends south and east through [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]] and into [[South Australia]], where it is found on the [[Eyre Peninsula]], [[Yorke Peninsula]], [[Kangaroo Island]], southern [[Mount Lofty Ranges]], and throughout the south-eastern region, where it is mostly restricted to sand dunes.<ref name=SA>{{cite web|url=http://www.flora.sa.gov.au/cgi-bin/speciesfacts_display.cgi?form=speciesfacts&name=Acacia_longifolia%20var.%20sophorae|title=''Acacia longifolia''|work=Electronic Flora of South Australia species Fact Sheet|access-date=29 March 2020|publisher=[[Government of South Australia]]}}</ref> The subspecies, ''A. sophorae'', grows in sand dunes around the [[Tasmania]]n coastline.

It has become [[naturalised]] in the south west of [[Western Australia]] in coastal areas extending from around [[Perth, Western Australia|Perth]] in the north down to around [[Albany, Western Australia|Albany]] in the south. It is thought to have been introduced by escaping from gardens or being used in revegetation plantings. Control methods include hand pulling seedlings, [[ringbarking]], or cutting the plant down and painting the stump with [[glyphosate]].<ref name=FloraBase>{{FloraBase|title=Acacia longifolia|id=17861}}</ref>

== Uses ==
''Acacia longifolia'' is widely cultivated in subtropical regions of the world. Its uses include prevention of soil erosion, food (flowers, seeds and seed pods), yellow [[dye]] (from the flowers), green dye (pods) and wood.<ref>Plants for a Future: [https://www.pfaf.org/database/plants.php?Acacia+longifolia ''Acacia longifolia'']</ref> The flower colour derives from the organic compound [[kaempferol]].<ref>Lycaeum: [http://users.lycaeum.org/~mulga/acacia/phyto.html Phytochemistry Intro] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930154547/http://users.lycaeum.org/~mulga/acacia/phyto.html |date=2007-09-30 }}</ref> The tree's bark has limited use in tanning, primarily for [[sheep]]skin. It is useful for securing uninhabited sand in coastal areas, primarily where there are not too many hard frosts.<ref>{{cite book|author=Ferdinand Mueller (freiherr von)|title=Select extra-tropical plants readily eligible for industrial culture or naturalization|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CfDcl2m-6BMC&pg=PA7|access-date=28 October 2010|year=1884|publisher=G.S. Davis|pages=7–}}</ref> In Tasmania the ripening pods were roasted and the seeds removed and eaten.<ref>{{cite book | author=J. H. Maiden | year=1889 | title=The useful native plants of Australia: Including Tasmania | publisher= Turner and Henderson, Sydney | url=https://primo-slnsw.hosted.exlibrisgroup.com/primo-explore/fulldisplay?docid=SLNSW_ALMA21105097830002626&context=L&vid=SLNSW&search_scope=EEA&tab=default_tab&lang=en_US}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
Despite its weed potential outside its normal range, the shrub is available commercially and can be propagated by seed [[scarification]] or boiling water treatment. It is regarded as an attractive, hardy, fast-growing species suitable as a hedge plant or for screening. Suitable for hydroseeding work on banks where it will provide soil stabilization. Sydney golden wattle is well suited for low maintenance areas such as road batters, will grow in a range of soil types and is [[frost]] hardy.<ref name=anh>{{cite web|url=https://www.anbg.gov.au/acacia/species/A-longifolia.html|title=''Acacia longifolia'' Sydney Golden Wattle|access-date=29 March 2020|work=Wattles - genus Acacia|publisher=[[Australian National Herbarium]]}}</ref> It is heavily used at present in Southern California as a street canopy tree, as it grows fairly quickly (reaching a height of five meters within a year or two of planting), tolerates drought, and is resilient even to the particularly brutal pruning practices associated with low-cost tree services.

In Portugal the species is considered highly invasive in sand dunes, and its cultivation is prohibited by law.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Extensive literature search for preparatory work to support pan European pest risk assessment: Trichilogaster acaciaelongifoliae. |year=2015 |url=https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2ad1/59da5a9bb07cc76532a5d5ab5ab810ba4b6d.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200209204615/https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2ad1/59da5a9bb07cc76532a5d5ab5ab810ba4b6d.pdf |archive-date=9 February 2020 |publisher=[[Wageningen University and Research]] |doi=10.2903/SP.EFSA.2015.EN-764 |s2cid=89213286 |access-date=11 February 2021|last1=Derkx |first1=M.P.M. |last2=Brouwer |first2=J.H.D. |last3=Van Breda |first3=P.J.M. |last4=Helsen |first4=H.H.M. |last5=Hoffman |first5=M.H.A. |last6=Hop |first6=M.E.C.M. |journal=EFSA Supporting Publications |volume=12 |issue=4 }}</ref>

== Invasive species ==
Originally from Australia, Acacia longifolia, sometimes known as Sydney golden wattle, is an invasive tree species that has spread to Mediterranean habitats, including Portuguese coastal dunes. Its quick growth, high seed output, and capacity to fix nitrogen allow it to outcompete native plants and change soil conditions, decreasing biodiversity and altering ecological processes. Originally, it was planted to stabilize sand dunes and prevent erosion.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Marchante |first=Hélia S. |last2=Marchante |first2=Elizabete M. |last3=Buscardo |first3=Erika |last4=Maia |first4=José |last5=Freitas |first5=Helena |date=2004 |title=Recovery Potential of Dune Ecosystems Invaded by an Exotic Acacia Species (Acacia longifolia) |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3989665 |journal=Weed Technology |volume=18 |pages=1427–1433 |issn=0890-037X}}</ref>

==Control==
In South Africa at least, the [[Pteromalidae|Pteromalid]] wasp ''[[Trichilogaster acaciaelongifoliae]]'' has been introduced from Australia, and has spread rapidly, achieving substantial control.<ref>Dennill, G.B.; The effect of the gall wasp Trichilogaster acaciaelongifoliae (Hymenoptera: Pteromalidae) on reproductive potential and vegetative growth of the weed Acacia longifolia; Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment, Volume 14, Issues 1-2, November 1985, Pages 53-61</ref> The effect on the trees has been described as drastic seed reduction (typically over 90%) by galling of reproductive buds, and indirect debilitation of the affected plant by increased abscission of inflorescences adjacent to the growing galls. The presence of galls also caused leaf abscission, reducing vegetative growth as well as reproductive output.
